concept.name: GraphQL Federation & Supergraph Routing

relationships.description: Connects GraphQL Federation to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Composing independent domain GraphQL subgraphs into one unified supergraph behind a stateless query-planning router.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of GraphQL Federation—from @key entity hydration and QueryPlan DAGs to Federation v2 @override migrations, APQ caching, and DataLoader N+1 defense.

spark.summary: GraphQL Federation composes multiple independent domain subgraphs into a single unified schema at a stateless router, letting teams deploy services separately while clients query one endpoint.
spark.keyTakeaway: Federation decouples schema ownership across teams without forcing clients to stitch APIs, provided you enforce strict subgraph composition checks and batch entity lookups.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** As a monolithic GraphQL server grows past 5–10 teams, schema merge conflicts and shared release trains stall delivery.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Stateless Router Hydrating @key Entities Across Subgraphs (Client App -> Federation Router -> Users Subgraph -> Orders Subgraph); APQ + Depth Guard -> Federation Router -> Batched Subgraph DataLoader (APQ + Cost Guard -> Rust QueryPlan Router -> Subgraph DataLoader -> Domain DB).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare Federation against hand-coded Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) aggregators and REST gateways. In production, a non-nullable cross-subgraph extension field (`user.loyaltyPoints: Int!`) will null out the entire parent `Order` response if the Loyalty subgraph times out.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how DataLoader fixes GraphQL N+1 storms and how HTTP/gRPC compare at the transport layer.

learningJourney.title: What is GraphQL Federation
learningJourney.explanation:
As a monolithic GraphQL server grows past 5–10 teams, schema merge conflicts and shared release trains stall delivery. **GraphQL Federation** lets each domain team own an independent **subgraph** (`Identity`, `Orders`, `Catalog`) exposing `_service { sdl }` and `_entities(representations: [_Any!]!)`.

A central schema registry composes subgraphs at build time into a **Supergraph SDL**. At runtime, a stateless **Router** (e.g., Apollo Router in Rust, WunderGraph Cosmo) compiles each query into a `QueryPlan` DAG (`Sequence`, `Parallel`, `Flatten` steps) across subgraphs.

sectionDiagram.title: Stateless Router Hydrating @key Entities Across Subgraphs
sectionDiagram.summary: The router injects __typename and @key fields automatically so downstream subgraphs can hydrate foreign types.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how GraphQL Federation works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why Federation Beats Manual Schema Stitching & Client Waterfalls
learningJourney.explanation: Mobile clients over cellular networks suffer when forced to make 4–6 sequential REST waterfalls (`GET /user` -> `GET /orders` -> `GET /products`). Federation collapses that into 1 external round trip while keeping backend teams independently deployable.

ideas.title: Federation v2 Explicit Directives
ideas.description: Use `@shareable` for multi-subgraph fields, `@external` + `@requires` for computed cross-subgraph fields, and `@override(from: "Monolith", label: "percent(10)")` for zero-downtime migrations.

ideas.title: Composition CI Gates
ideas.description: Run `rover subgraph check` in every subgraph PR against the production supergraph so breaking schema changes never reach deployment.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Why Federation Beats Manual Schema Stitching & Client Waterfalls under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Federation Fits (and Where a Monolith or gRPC Wins)
learningJourney.explanation: Federation is an organizational scaling tool—don't pay its network-hop and query-planning tax for a single small team.

benefits: Autonomous teams (`Identity`, `Catalog`, `Checkout`) deploy independently behind one unified client graph.
costs: Deeply nested `@requires` chains create `Sequence` steps in `QueryPlan`, adding inter-subgraph RTT.

benefits: A modular monolith with one GraphQL server avoids extra network hops and distributed tracing.
costs: Splitting a 3-person team into 4 federated subgraphs adds pure latency and ops overhead.

benefits: gRPC + Protobuf delivers 5–10x lower serialization overhead and strict binary streaming.
costs: `POST /graphql` JSON payloads are suboptimal for service-to-service telemetry streams.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Entity Keys (@key), @requires & Subgraph DataLoader Batching
learningJourney.explanation: Every `__resolveReference` resolver receives a batch of entity representations from the router—always wrap database/RPC lookups inside a request-scoped **DataLoader** to prevent an N+1 query storm.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```graphql
# Identity Subgraph
type User @key(fields: "id") {
  id: ID!
  email: String!
}

# Checkout Subgraph extending User with computed shipping tier
type User @key(fields: "id") {
  id: ID!
  country: String! @external
  orders(first: Int = 10): [Order!]!
  freeShippingEligible: Boolean! @requires(fields: "country")
}
```
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: GraphQL Federation vs. REST BFF vs. gRPC Gateway
learningJourney.explanation: Compare Federation against hand-coded Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) aggregators and REST gateways.

benefits: Declarative query planning, automatic entity batching, and Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) via SHA-256.
costs: `POST /graphql` defeats standard URL-based CDN caching unless using APQ over GET.

benefits: Full control over parallel RPCs, HTTP `Cache-Control` headers, and static payload shapes.
costs: Every new mobile screen requires writing and deploying custom BFF aggregation endpoints.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production Hardening: Depth Limits, Nullable Extensions & DataLoader
learningJourney.explanation: In production, a non-nullable cross-subgraph extension field (`user.loyaltyPoints: Int!`) will null out the entire parent `Order` response if the Loyalty subgraph times out. Keep cross-subgraph extensions nullable, enforce static depth/cost limits (`maxDepth=8`), and set per-subgraph timeouts.

sectionDiagram.title: APQ + Depth Guard -> Federation Router -> Batched Subgraph DataLoader

cards.label: N+1 Defense
cards.detail: DataLoader coalesces 50 entity keys into a single WHERE id IN (...) DB query.

cards.label: Partial Failure
cards.detail: Nullable extension fields isolate subgraph timeouts without crashing the whole response.

cards.label: DoS Protection
cards.detail: Static query depth (<=8), alias caps, and demand-cost budgets block abusive queries.

sectionDiagram.summary: Batched DataLoaders, nullable subgraph extensions, and query cost limits keep federated graphs fast and resilient.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a federated GraphQL supergraph, why should cross-subgraph extension fields (e.g., `Order.loyaltyPoints` hydrated by a separate Loyalty subgraph) generally be nullable?

options.text: Because GraphQL error-bubbling rules will null out the entire parent `Order` object if a non-nullable extension field fails or times out
options.feedback: Correct: nullable extension fields contain partial failures to just that field instead of failing the entire checkout response.

options.text: Because Federation v2 forbids non-nullable types in `@key` definitions
options.feedback: `@key` fields like `id: ID!` are non-nullable; it is cross-subgraph extension fields that benefit from nullability.

options.text: Because DataLoader only batches nullable fields

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
